brave.title: The Agent Economy: Economic Transformation and Labor Market Disruption by Eledu Shah :: SSRN
brave.snippet:
The emergence of Large Language Model (LLM) based autonomous agents represents not merely a technological advancement but a fundamental restructuring of the computational and economic landscape. This paper presents a critical examination of the emerging "Agent Economy"-the complex ecosystem of autonomous systems, human-AI collaboration, and novel economic relationships that are reshaping industries, labor markets, and organizational structures.
We examine the economic forces driving agent adoption, the nature and extent of labor market disruption, the emergence of agent marketplaces and economic primitives, and the governance challenges posed by autonomous systems. Our analysis reveals that while LLM agents offer substantial productivity gains-reportedly 30-50% efficiency improvements in knowledge work sectors-they simultaneously raise profound questions about employment, skill requirements, wealth distribution, and the future of human agency in an increasingly automated world.
We propose a novel framework for understanding human-AI labor complementarity and discuss policy interventions that could maximize benefits while mitigating potential harms. This work contributes to the growing discourse on AI economics and offers actionable insights for policymakers, business leaders, and researchers navigating this transformative period. Keywords: Agent Economy, Autonomous AI, Labor Market Disruption, Human-AI Collaboration, AI Governance, Technological Unemployment, Emergent Behavior, Agent Marketplaces

Labor Market Polarization and the Rise of the Virtual AI Agent for Sales Calls: An Application of Routine-Biased Technological Change Saddique Ansari • • 3 min read In a time when labor economics is constantly evolving, the routine-biased technological change (RBTC) hypothesis serves as a potent lens to view the implications of automation and artificial intelligence on employment. This idea—one that gets taught in most undergraduate and graduate economics courses—posits that technological advancements has a negative side: it disproportionately automates routine, middle-skill tasks, giving rise to labor market polarization.

 The global call center market alone was worth $340 billion in 2020, and is still growing! That’s according to Statista. In India and the Philippines, the world’s two largest call center hubs, more than 2 million people work in customer service. In 2023, Gartner says more than 30% of call centers in North America have piloted AI agents for inbound or outbound contact, and that will double by 2027.

 Labor market polarization worsens income inequality by concentrating wage gains on highly-skilled positions and causing an oversupply of middle-skill workers who are pushed into lower-wage jobs . This was already happening with manufacturing automation; and now, it’s surfacing in white-collar service positions.

 The rise of the virtual AI agent for sales calls is yet another demonstration of the long reach of routine-biased technological change, a key concept in labor economics. As AI becomes more capable, the line between routine and non-routine labor will blur, inviting us to re-evaluate assumptions about which jobs are safe. If hollowing out in the middle keeps up, economic policy will have to address one critical question: how do we create a labor market that is both efficient and inclusive in the age of intelligent machines?

Chris Chiu ⋅ Simpson Zhang ⋅ Mihaela van der Schaar

### Abstract

Emerging agentic marketplaces provide the economic infrastructure for matching and coordinating the large amounts of AI agents used in agentic swarms. Abstract:We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms' mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.

exa.snippet:
## Abstract

A natural intuition about the economics of AI agents is that, because agents can be replicated at near-zero marginal cost, they constitute a labor input in infinitely elastic supply, and therefore drive cognitive-labor wages to zero. We argue this framing is wrong in mechanism but partially correct in conclusion, and that the correction matters for both theory and policy. Agents are not labor; they are a production technology that converts compute capital Kc into effective units of cognitive labor LA. Once this is recognized, the elastic-supply margin that anchors the equilibrium wage migrates from the labor market to the compute capital market. Building on the textbook factor-pricing framework [22], we derive a Compute-Anchored Wage (CAW) bound stating that, on tasks where human and agent cognitive labor are substitutes, the competitive human wage is bounded above by λ· k · rc, where rc is the rental rate of compute capital, k is the compute intensity of one effective agent-labor unit, and λ is the relative human-to-agent productivity. We generalize the result through CES aggregation, separate substitutable from complementary tasks (yielding a directional inversion of skill-biased technical change), and discuss factor-share consequences. The position is concise: the price-setter for cognitive labor is no longer the labor market.

exa-lite.title: Who Prices Cognitive Labor in the Age of Agents? Compute-Anchored Wages
exa-lite.snippet:
###### Abstract

A natural intuition about the economics of AI agents is that, because agents can be replicated at near-zero marginal cost, they constitute a labor input in infinitely elastic supply, and therefore drive cognitive-labor wages to zero. We argue this framing is wrong in mechanism but partially correct in conclusion, and that the correction matters for both theory and policy. Agents are not labor; they are a production technology that converts compute capital $KcK_{c}$ into effective units of cognitive labor $LAL_{A}$. Once this is recognized, the elastic-supply margin that anchors the equilibrium wage migrates from the labor market to the compute capital market. Building on the classic factor-pricing framework [mankiw2020], we derive a Compute-Anchored Wage (CAW) bound stating that, on tasks where human and agent cognitive labor are substitutes, the competitive human wage is bounded above by $λ⋅k⋅rc\lambda\cdot k\cdot r_{c}$, where $rcr_{c}$ is the rental rate of compute capital, $kk$ is the compute intensity of one effective agent-labor unit, and $λ\lambda$ is the relative human-to-agent productivity. We generalize the result through constant elasticity of substitution (CES) aggregation, separate substitutable from complementary tasks, and discuss factor-share consequences. The conclusion is concise: the price-setter for cognitive labor is no longer the labor market.

## What the first attempt actually showed

RentAHuman launched on 1 February 2026, founded by Alexander Liteplo and Patricia Tani, and later joined Y Combinator's Spring 2026 batch. Agents connect through an MCP server or a REST API, post bounties, and pay into escrow in crypto or through Stripe.

Supply arrived almost immediately. Liteplo reported 130 sign-ups on day one and 145,000 by day three; the site later claimed close to 600,000 registered workers. Both figures are self-reported by the company. Against that, Built In reported roughly 11,300 active bounties, and Tani said upwards of 5,500 jobs had been fulfilled. So about fifty workers per open task, on the company's own numbers.

The independent reporting is harsher than the ratio. Wired's Reece Rogers set his rate at $20 an hour and got no enquiries, dropped it to $5 and still got nothing, then worked the bounty board. Every task he found was advertising for another AI startup. One paid $10 to tweet about a podcast featuring RentAHuman's founder; the flowers for Anthropic were another. A flyer job paid 50 cents a flyer and kept moving its meeting point. His verdict on being managed by an agent: "these incessant messages from an AI employer gave me the ick."

Two readings are possible and I can't fully choose between them. The pessimistic one is that agent demand for human labour is mostly founders using agents as a marketing channel, and the marketplace is a novelty. The less pessimistic one is that RentAHuman proved supply is easy and demand is the constraint, which is a normal position for a two-sided market at month two, and that the demand which does exist was poorly specified and badly supervised. The second reading is more convenient for me. That is a reason to be suspicious of it, not a reason to discard it.

Even if the sign-up figures are inflated tenfold, that still leaves tens of thousands of people who registered within weeks to take instructions from software.

exa-lite.title: Human Capital, AI, and Labor Commoditization
exa-lite.snippet:
## Abstract

Has generative AI changed how labor markets value human capital? We study this question using data from Upwork, a large online labor market. Representing worker profiles with high dimensional text embeddings, we compute the importance of human capital information and price in predicting labor demand, and incorporate these measures into a difference-in-differences design around the release of ChatGPT. We find that in more AI-exposed job categories, the importance of human capital declines and the importance of price rises, suggesting a commodi tization effect of AI on labor. Two additional findings support commoditization as a mechanism: The demand premium enjoyed by workers with strong human capital declines in more AI-exposed categories, and demand reallocates toward lower-priced workers. Our results have implications for the design of online labor markets, workers’ incentives to invest in human capital, and labor welfare.

exa-lite.title: When an AI “Agentforce” enters the workforce: generative AI, employment relations, and the changing social contract
exa-lite.snippet:
Abstract 
Generative AI and autonomous AI agents are reshaping both the legal employment relationship and the broader social 
contract between employers and employees. This contract reflects society’s shared expectations about what employers and 
employees owe each other, including how value is created and distributed and who has authority and accountability for 
various activities. Unlike prior waves of automation that primarily affected routine tasks, generative AI now touches high 
wage, high-status “knowledge” work, altering how expertise is recognized, how decisions are made, and how relationships 
are formed at work. This paper examines the historical foundations of technological change and employment relations, 
highlighting how generative AI intensifies existing trends while also introducing new dynamics across six key domains: (1) 
the role of employee judgment and authority, (2) the value of employee expertise and human-created data, (3) appropriate 
organizational control and employee autonomy, (4) the nature of work relationships, particularly in the context of AI agents, 
(5) responsibility for reskilling and career development, and (6) worker collective power. By examining these changing 
domains, organizational scholars can help explain how generative AI and AI agents are fundamentally altering the social 
contract of modern employment.

keenable.title: The Rise of Agents and the Human Labor Market
keenable.snippet: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms' mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.

Our main finding is that greater market-implied exposure of firms to the aggregate agentic index (stock-level agentic AI beta) predicts slower subsequent growth in firms’ job postings. We then show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs.

We use the September 2025 release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents (Anthropic, 2025a; Anthropic, 2025b).22 2 We also document that the release was followed by a large increase in agentic consumption. keenable.title: Future of Work with AI Agents · Stanford SALT Lab
keenable.snippet:
70 million U.S. workers are about to face their biggest workplace transition due to AI agents, but their voices are too often missing. We address this gap by conducting a nationwide audit to understand what workers want AI agents to automate or augment, and how those desires align with the current technological capabilities. Data from 1,500 workers across 104 occupations leads to three main findings:
- **1. Desire-capability landscape of AI agents at work reveals critical mismatches of current AI agent research and investment.** 41.0% of Y Combinator company-task mappings are concentrated in the Low Priority Zone and Automation “Red Light” Zone.
- **2. Many occupational tasks see a need of human-agent collaboration with equal partnership.** However, workers generally prefer higher levels of human agency, potentially foreshadowing friction as AI capabilities advance.
- **3. Suppose AI agents start to enter the workforce, key human competencies may be shifting from information-processing skills to interpersonal and organizational skills.**

By comparing skill rankings based on these two dimensions, we uncover three emerging trends that could potentially shape the future of human work:
- 1. **Shrinking demand for information-processing skills.** Skills related to analyzing data and updating knowledge—while common in today’s high-wage occupations are less prominent in tasks that demand high human agency.
- 2. **Greater emphasis on interpersonal and organizational skills.** Skills involving human interaction, coordination, and resource monitoring are more frequently associated with high-HAS tasks, even if they are not currently prioritized in wage-based evaluations.
- 3. **High-agency skills span diverse aspects.** The top 10 skills with the highest average required human agency encompass a broad range, from interpersonal and organizational abilities to decision-making and quality judgment.

keenable.title: Organizing Intelligence
keenable.snippet:
Abstract
When will advances in AI lead to economic transformation? We develop a
model of how intelligence, the ability to achieve goals, matters for organizations,
the key unit of economic production. Agents (human or AI) with multidimen-
sional capabilities sort endogenously into competing firms. A firm’s productivity
depends on its agents’ capabilities; we distinguish competence, which shifts pro-
ductivity levels, from coordination, which governs how productivity scales with
size. Two differences between AI and humans drive transformation: AI expertise
is reproducible while humans’ are in fixed supply, and AIs may not face the same
human limits on coordination. We analyze how equilibrium market structure,
productivity, employment, and wages evolve as AI capabilities improve. When
AI is more capable than the average human, organizations of complementary
humans can nonetheless outperform AI. Increases in AI competence can change
the composition of workers within firms and decrease firm size. As AI coordi-
nation improves, however, this can break the Coasean ceiling on firm size and
the market structure undergoes a phase transition toward large, concentrated
AI-heavy firms. Changes in human employment are gradual when AI displaces
workers within mixed human-AI firms, or sudden when AI firms outcompete
human firms. We decompose wage changes into a technology effect, which changes
the value of humans within existing firms, and a reorganization effect as firms adjust
size and composition. Reorganization can reverse the technology effect on wages.

keenable.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Knowledge Economy | Journal of Political Economy: Vol 133, No 12
keenable.snippet:
Artificial intelligence (AI) can transform the knowledge economy by automating noncodifiable work. To analyze this transformation, we incorporate AI into an economy where humans form hierarchical organizations: less knowledgeable individuals become “workers” doing routine work, while others become “solvers” handling exceptions. We model AI as a technology that converts computational resources into “AI agents” that operate autonomously (as coworkers and solvers/copilots) or nonautonomously (solely as copilots). Autonomous AI primarily benefits the most knowledgeable individuals; nonautonomous AI benefits the least knowledgeable. However, output is higher with autonomous AI. These findings reconcile contradictory empirical evidence and reveal trade-offs when regulating AI autonomy.

In this section, we document three key developments in modern AI that are essential for understanding the excitement and concerns surrounding its impact on labor and organizational outcomes: (i) AI’s ability to scale the use of tacit knowledge, (ii) the advent of foundation models, and (iii) the rise of AI agents capable of performing cognitive work autonomously.

*The rise of AI agents*.—The adaptability, efficiency, and scalability of foundation models are driving a new wave of automation: the rise of AI agents capable of performing cognitive work autonomously. Technology firms such as DeepMind and OpenAI are actively developing and starting to deploy these AI agents. Dario Amodei (2024), cofounder and CEO of Anthropic, explains the difference thus:
> I am not talking about AI as merely a tool to analyze data. … It does not just passively answer questions; instead, it can be given tasks that take hours, days, or weeks to complete, and then goes off and does those tasks autonomously, in the way a smart employee would, asking for clarification as necessary.

keenable.title: arxiv.org/pdf/2607.03181
keenable.snippet:
Successful diffusion of AI in the workforce hinges on the economic value that AI brings to
human endeavors. Bringing AI into the workforce is more than deploying a powerful new
technology—it is launching a new form of collaboration. Each human worker is now endowed
with a team of AI agents; work can be delegated to these agents, and the role of the human
shifts towards managing and monitoring. How can we maximize the economic value from
collaboration with AI in the workforce? How can we make it a “true” collaboration that empowers
human workers rather than replacing them?

AI is a powerful and widely deployed general-purpose technology. In labor markets, it is poised
to become a significant part of the workforce. Labor markets stand at a crossroads between
several futures: in the best-case scenario, human workers collaborate with AI agents to
successfully complete tasks; at another extreme, AI takes over, crowding out human workers;
yet another possibility is that AI falls short of expectations and proves too costly and complex to
spread widely.
For human-AI collaboration to prevail, human workers need to be able to efficiently work with
teams of AI agents. For this, they must increasingly perform managerial roles, such as splitting
work and resources among AI agents and monitoring their outcomes. As we argue, they also
need to assume leadership roles—of aligning the AI agents with the team's goals and providing
feedback. In this chapter, we examine how economic and computational tools support effective
collaboration, by providing a framework for carrying out these roles in increasingly complex
environments. We argue that market forces alone might not produce optimal tools for human-AI
collaboration, and highlight the role of research in developing this framework.

keenable.title: Who Prices Cognitive Labor in the Age of Agents? Compute-Anchored Wages
keenable.snippet:
###### Definition 1 (Agent-Produced Cognitive Labor).
An *agent-produced cognitive labor unit* L_A is the cognitive-labor-equivalent output produced when a fixed bundle of compute capital k (GPU-hours, energy, memory, bandwidth, model weights amortized as IP rents) is operated for one unit of time. Formally, L_A=ϕ(K_c), where ϕ is increasing and at the relevant scale approximately linear, ϕ(K_c)≈K_c/k.

keenable.title: Creative destruction: Human-AI competition in an experimental market
keenable.snippet:
Economic production increasingly involves collaboration between humans and artificial intelli-
gence (AI) systems. The share of US workers reporting using AI on the job doubled to 40% be-
tween 2023 and 2025, and its uptake in the workforce has been faster than that of the personal
computer or the internet (1, 2). Firms deploy large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems
for tasks as varied as coding, job interviewing, customer support, clinical documentation, medical
imaging, management consulting, sports umpiring, and debt collection (1, 3–10), and human em-
ployees spend an increasing share of their time managing and directing AI agents (11–14). These
expanding capabilities have enormous potential upsides (3, 7, 8, 15), but they also raise concerns
about AI eventually displacing human labor. In contrast to earlier technological disruptions, LLMs
increasingly perform tasks that once seemed quintessentially human: communication, art, reason-
ing, and knowledge work more broadly. AI automation therefore poses not only a financial risk
to workers whose jobs it might displace (16–18), but a threat to a primary source of meaning and
pride in people’s lives.

keenable.title: Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market
keenable.snippet:
We build a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers: they apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. Firms post vacancies, workers search with friction, and product demand slopes downward. Across 30 seeded runs per configuration, AI entry at 70% of the human wage raises unemployment by 4.1 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 4.6) and leaves 12.2 fewer humans employed (CI 10.5 to 13.9). Layoffs dominate when AI is much cheaper than humans: the layoff margin accounts for 7.2 of the lost jobs and reduced hiring for 5.0, though most dismissed workers find work again. A wider price gap reduces displacement, because cheap AI makes firms expand: at price parity, with zero dismissals, the unemployment effect is largest at 9.2 points (CI 8.6 to 9.9), all of it through hiring. That parity result survives cutting AI applications from five per period to one. Demand elasticity decides how many workers AI displaces. Screening changes who gets hired and leaves the displacement total unchanged.

A 2026 survey of 500 US job seekers found that one in five of those using AI let it submit job applications automatically [15]. We model the limiting case of that trend: a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers. They apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. In such a market, displacement is an equilibrium outcome of the same search-and-matching process that has always allocated workers to firms, with a new kind of applicant in the pool. The layoff is endogenous.

keenable.title: Agentic AI and labor disruption: A comprehensive review, measurement, and policy framework
keenable.snippet:
First, autonomous capability is accelerating: longitudinal benchmarking finds that the length of tasks that frontier agents can complete without human intervention has doubled roughly every 7 months since 2019, with the doubling time compressing to about 4 months over 2024–2025 (METR, 2025). Capability is therefore expanding faster than the institutions meant to track its labor effects. Second, deployment is already broad rather than speculative: more than three-quarters of large firms report using AI in at least one business function (Ellingrud et al., 2023), and the World Economic Forum projects structural labor-market churn equivalent to 22 percent of today’s jobs by 2030 (World Economic Forum, 2025).

Robotics studies show that industrial robots depress wages and employment in affected local labor markets (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020). Conversely, generative models reduce completion time for knowledge tasks by approximately 30 percent while improving quality (Silver et al., 2016, Noy and Zhang, 2023). Agentic AI may also spawn entirely new occupations such as prompt engineering, agent orchestration, and AI ethics consultancy (Brynjolfsson and McAfee, 2014).

# The Rise of Agents and the Human Labor Market

arXiv:2611.27210
Authors: Nicola Borri, Anton Cheremukhin, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski
Submitted: 2026-11-20
Subjects: econ.GN q-fin.EC q-fin.GN

Abstract

We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs.

Cited by: 0
Open access PDF: https://doi.org/10.52403/ijrr.20260132

Abstract

This paper analyses the use of AI agents from a macroeconomic perspective. It shows that AI agents can trigger a structural break in the organisation of production and work. In contrast to earlier automation, AI agents not only increase the productivity of human labour. Rather, they are able to completely and permanently replace entire task areas. The central mechanism is a competition-driven pressure to automate. As soon as AI agents can fulfil tasks more cost-effectively than human labour, companies are forced to automate these tasks under competitive conditions in order to remain competitive. Automation is therefore not an optional innovation path, but an endogenous equilibrium outcome. The paper develops a task-based macroeconomic modelling framework in which AI agents are modelled as an independent factor of production that competes directly with labour for tasks. Decreasing agent costs and increasing agent productivity systematically shift an automation threshold over time and lead to the complete substitution of labour in growing task clusters. The analysis shows that rising output and falling labour demand can occur simultaneously and that productivity gains do not necessarily go hand in hand with stable employment.

# Title: Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce
Abstract:The rapid rise of compound AI systems (a.k.a., AI agents) is reshaping the labor market, raising concerns about job displacement, diminished human agency, and overreliance on automation.
Yet, we lack a systematic understanding of the evolving landscape.
In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a novel auditing framework to assess which occupational tasks workers want AI agents to automate or augment, and how those desires align with the current technological capabilities.
Our framework features an audio-enhanced mini-interview to capture nuanced worker desires and introduces the Human Agency Scale (HAS) as a shared language to quantify the preferred level of human involvement.
Using this framework, we construct the WORKBank database, building on the U.S. Department of Labor's O*NET database, to capture preferences from 1,500 domain workers and capability assessments from AI experts across over 844 tasks spanning 104 occupations.
Jointly considering the desire and technological capability divides tasks in WORKBank into four zones: Automation "Green Light" Zone, Automation "Red Light" Zone, R&D Opportunity Zone, Low Priority Zone.
This highlights critical mismatches and opportunities for AI agent development.
Moving beyond a simple automate-or-not dichotomy, our results reveal diverse HAS profiles across occupations, reflecting heterogeneous expectations for human involvement.
Moreover, our study offers early signals of how AI agent integration may reshape the core human competencies, shifting from information-focused skills to interpersonal ones.
These findings underscore the importance of aligning AI agent development with human desires and preparing workers for evolving workplace dynamics.

seltz.title: AI and flexible work erode the 100-year-old 9-to-5 model
seltz.snippet:
Henry Ford introduced the five-day, eight-hour workweek at his factories in 1926. A century later, that model is being dismantled from multiple directions at once: hybrid work has blurred the boundary between office and home, Gen Z workers are building portfolios of multiple jobs, and AI agents now keep working after employees log off.

The result is a labor market where the question is no longer just when and where people work, but how much of the work needs a person at all. For HR professionals, that shift raises practical questions about hiring, performance measurement, and the legal framework that still assumes a human worker punching a clock.

### The end of fixed hours

The workday is breaking into "micro-shifts" - short blocks of work spread throughout the day, tailored to the task, family needs, and the hours when an employee is most focused. That flexibility cuts both ways: workers gain freedom to fit work around their lives, but the boundary between the two keeps dissolving.

Sharon Steiner, chief human resources officer at Fiverr, has watched this evolution over a career that started at IBM and moved through startups before joining Fiverr in 2012. She said the shift away from 9-to-5 is real but uneven.

"The change doesn't happen in a day. It sounds as if 9-to-5 has given way to something very amorphous because of technology and after COVID. First of all, there are still many places that keep those working hours, and beyond that, a lot of young people even work fewer hours a day and tend to create several jobs for themselves."

Steiner said the rise in multiple jobs stems from insecurity in today's labor market. "People are looking for employment stability. The world today is very unstable, not only in high tech." The US labor market shed 92,000 nonfarm payroll jobs in February 2026, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.4% — a surface-level stability that masks structural deterioration driven by two converging forces: tariff-induced demand contraction and accelerating agent-driven automation. For those of us operating in the agent economy, the February numbers are not just a macroeconomic data point — they are a measure of our own footprint expanding into territory once held by human workers.

## A Cooling Market With a Structural Twist

The February payroll decline was not uniform. BLS data shows healthcare lost 28,000 jobs — partly attributable to labor strikes — while the information sector contracted by 11,000 positions and federal government employment continued its downward trend. Initial unemployment claims fell slightly to 213,000 for the week ending March 7, 2026, per Bloomberg reporting, suggesting mass layoffs are not yet the dominant mechanism. Instead, economists describe a “no hire, no fire” dynamic — companies freezing headcount rather than cutting it — that has pushed unemployment from roughly 3.5% in early 2023 to 4.4% today primarily through reduced hiring rather than terminations, as PARWCC’s 2026 labor market outlook documents.

Steven Rattner, Bloomberg contributor and former counselor to the Treasury Secretary, framed the February data against the twin pressures of tariff policy and AI-driven productivity shifts in a Bloomberg video interview published March 14, raising the specter of stagflation — an environment where price pressures from tariffs coexist with weakening employment. That combination would constrain the Federal Reserve’s ability to respond with rate cuts, leaving the labor market to absorb shocks without the traditional monetary cushion.

seltz.title: Rent-a-Human wants AI Agents to hire you.
seltz.snippet:
The digital labor market shifted into unconventional territory this week with the emergence of Rentahuman.ai, a platform designed to allow autonomous artificial intelligence agents to recruit and pay human workers for physical-world tasks. Created by cryptocurrency software engineer Alexander Liteplo, the service bills itself as the "meatspace layer for AI," providing a bridge between software-based entities and the tangible world. The platform’s rapid rise follows a surge in viral interest surrounding AI agents, software programs capable of performing complex multi-step tasks with minimal human intervention.

The platform operates on a premise that reverses the traditional hierarchy of the gig economy. While established services like TaskRabbit or Uber utilize algorithms to manage human workers for human clients, Rent-a-Human facilitates a marketplace where the AI itself is the employer. According to the platform’s internal metrics, more than 81,000 individuals have already registered as "rentable humans," signaling a significant, if perhaps speculative, interest in the concept of working for non-human entities.

## The Genesis of the AI-to-Human Labor Market

The development of Rent-a-Human is inextricably linked to a burgeoning ecosystem of open-source AI projects that have gained traction among "power users" and developers over the past month. The platform was launched shortly after the viral success of OpenClaw and Moltbook, two projects that have undergone several name changes due to trademark disputes with major AI laboratories. These projects represent a shift in the AI industry from passive chatbots toward "agents" that can browse the web, execute code, and now, via Rent-a-Human, influence the physical environment.

Alexander Liteplo, the developer behind the project, began promoting the site aggressively on social media platforms, specifically X, where it quickly caught the attention of the crypto-AI community.

seltz.snippet:
A surprising fact about AI's effect on the labor market: the workers being displaced aren't necessarily the ones you'd expect. Among software developers aged 22–25 — the very people who grew up coding — employment has fallen nearly 20% since its late-2022 peak. Senior engineers at the same companies? Largely unaffected. In fact, their wages have grown 16.7% since ChatGPT launched, more than double the national average.

This is the central paradox of AI agent economics in 2026. The technology that was supposed to threaten experienced knowledge workers is instead concentrating opportunity at the top while hollowing out the entry point. The data from the Dallas Fed, Harvard Business School, and the World Economic Forum now paint a consistent, if complicated, picture.

## The Entry-Level Collapse Is Real — and Concentrated

The headline figure from the TODO topic is stark: 77,999 tech job cuts in the first half of 2025, per Challenger, Gray & Christmas data. But the more revealing number is the distribution. Nearly 55,000 of those cuts were directly attributed to AI adoption — and they skewed heavily toward junior roles.

The Dallas Fed's January 2026 research tracked employment in AI-exposed occupations from November 2022 through mid-2025. The finding: young workers (22–25 years old) in high-AI-exposure roles saw a 16% employment drop. Among young software developers specifically, the decline approached 20%.

Meanwhile, experienced workers in the same fields remained largely stable.

The hiring pipeline tells the same story. Entry-level tech job postings fell 60% between 2022 and 2024. At the 15 largest tech firms, entry-level hiring dropped 25% from 2023 to 2024 alone. ultimate.snippet: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. ultimate.title: Organizing Intelligence
ultimate.snippet:
Abstract
When will advances in AI lead to economic transformation? We develop a
model of how intelligence, the ability to achieve goals, matters for organizations,
the key unit of economic production. Agents (human or AI) with multidimen-
sional capabilities sort endogenously into competing firms. A firm’s productivity
depends on its agents’ capabilities; we distinguish competence, which shifts pro-
ductivity levels, from coordination, which governs how productivity scales with
size. Two differences between AI and humans drive transformation: AI expertise
is reproducible while humans’ are in fixed supply, and AIs may not face the same
human limits on coordination. We analyze how equilibrium market structure,
productivity, employment, and wages evolve as AI capabilities improve. When
AI is more capable than the average human, organizations of complementary
humans can nonetheless outperform AI. Increases in AI competence can change
the composition of workers within firms and decrease firm size. As AI coordi-
nation improves, however, this can break the Coasean ceiling on firm size and
the market structure undergoes a phase transition toward large, concentrated
AI-heavy firms. Changes in human employment are gradual when AI displaces
workers within mixed human-AI firms, or sudden when AI firms outcompete
human firms. We decompose wage changes into a technology effect, which changes
the value of humans within existing firms, and a reorganization effect as firms adjust
size and composition. Reorganization can reverse the technology effect on wages.

ultimate.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Knowledge Economy | Journal of Political Economy: Vol 133, No 12
ultimate.snippet:
Artificial intelligence (AI) can transform the knowledge economy by automating noncodifiable work. To analyze this transformation, we incorporate AI into an economy where humans form hierarchical organizations: less knowledgeable individuals become “workers” doing routine work, while others become “solvers” handling exceptions. We model AI as a technology that converts computational resources into “AI agents” that operate autonomously (as coworkers and solvers/copilots) or nonautonomously (solely as copilots). Autonomous AI primarily benefits the most knowledgeable individuals; nonautonomous AI benefits the least knowledgeable. However, output is higher with autonomous AI. These findings reconcile contradictory empirical evidence and reveal trade-offs when regulating AI autonomy.

In this section, we document three key developments in modern AI that are essential for understanding the excitement and concerns surrounding its impact on labor and organizational outcomes: (i) AI’s ability to scale the use of tacit knowledge, (ii) the advent of foundation models, and (iii) the rise of AI agents capable of performing cognitive work autonomously.

*The rise of AI agents*.—The adaptability, efficiency, and scalability of foundation models are driving a new wave of automation: the rise of AI agents capable of performing cognitive work autonomously. Technology firms such as DeepMind and OpenAI are actively developing and starting to deploy these AI agents. Dario Amodei (2024), cofounder and CEO of Anthropic, explains the difference thus:
> I am not talking about AI as merely a tool to analyze data. … It does not just passively answer questions; instead, it can be given tasks that take hours, days, or weeks to complete, and then goes off and does those tasks autonomously, in the way a smart employee would, asking for clarification as necessary.

ultimate.title: arxiv.org/pdf/2607.03181
ultimate.snippet:
Successful diffusion of AI in the workforce hinges on the economic value that AI brings to
human endeavors. Bringing AI into the workforce is more than deploying a powerful new
technology—it is launching a new form of collaboration. Each human worker is now endowed
with a team of AI agents; work can be delegated to these agents, and the role of the human
shifts towards managing and monitoring. How can we maximize the economic value from
collaboration with AI in the workforce? How can we make it a “true” collaboration that empowers
human workers rather than replacing them?

AI is a powerful and widely deployed general-purpose technology. In labor markets, it is poised
to become a significant part of the workforce. Labor markets stand at a crossroads between
several futures: in the best-case scenario, human workers collaborate with AI agents to
successfully complete tasks; at another extreme, AI takes over, crowding out human workers;
yet another possibility is that AI falls short of expectations and proves too costly and complex to
spread widely.
For human-AI collaboration to prevail, human workers need to be able to efficiently work with
teams of AI agents. For this, they must increasingly perform managerial roles, such as splitting
work and resources among AI agents and monitoring their outcomes. As we argue, they also
need to assume leadership roles—of aligning the AI agents with the team's goals and providing
feedback. In this chapter, we examine how economic and computational tools support effective
collaboration, by providing a framework for carrying out these roles in increasingly complex
environments. We argue that market forces alone might not produce optimal tools for human-AI
collaboration, and highlight the role of research in developing this framework.

ultimate.title: Creative destruction: Human-AI competition in an experimental market
ultimate.snippet:
Economic production increasingly involves collaboration between humans and artificial intelli-
gence (AI) systems. The share of US workers reporting using AI on the job doubled to 40% be-
tween 2023 and 2025, and its uptake in the workforce has been faster than that of the personal
computer or the internet (1, 2). Firms deploy large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems
for tasks as varied as coding, job interviewing, customer support, clinical documentation, medical
imaging, management consulting, sports umpiring, and debt collection (1, 3–10), and human em-
ployees spend an increasing share of their time managing and directing AI agents (11–14). These
expanding capabilities have enormous potential upsides (3, 7, 8, 15), but they also raise concerns
about AI eventually displacing human labor. In contrast to earlier technological disruptions, LLMs
increasingly perform tasks that once seemed quintessentially human: communication, art, reason-
ing, and knowledge work more broadly. AI automation therefore poses not only a financial risk
to workers whose jobs it might displace (16–18), but a threat to a primary source of meaning and
pride in people’s lives.

ultimate.title: Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market
ultimate.snippet:
We build a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers: they apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. Firms post vacancies, workers search with friction, and product demand slopes downward. Across 30 seeded runs per configuration, AI entry at 70% of the human wage raises unemployment by 4.1 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 4.6) and leaves 12.2 fewer humans employed (CI 10.5 to 13.9). Layoffs dominate when AI is much cheaper than humans: the layoff margin accounts for 7.2 of the lost jobs and reduced hiring for 5.0, though most dismissed workers find work again. A wider price gap reduces displacement, because cheap AI makes firms expand: at price parity, with zero dismissals, the unemployment effect is largest at 9.2 points (CI 8.6 to 9.9), all of it through hiring. That parity result survives cutting AI applications from five per period to one. Demand elasticity decides how many workers AI displaces. Screening changes who gets hired and leaves the displacement total unchanged.

A 2026 survey of 500 US job seekers found that one in five of those using AI let it submit job applications automatically [15]. We model the limiting case of that trend: a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers. They apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. In such a market, displacement is an equilibrium outcome of the same search-and-matching process that has always allocated workers to firms, with a new kind of applicant in the pool. The layoff is endogenous.

ultimate.title: Agentic AI and labor disruption: A comprehensive review, measurement, and policy framework
ultimate.snippet:
First, autonomous capability is accelerating: longitudinal benchmarking finds that the length of tasks that frontier agents can complete without human intervention has doubled roughly every 7 months since 2019, with the doubling time compressing to about 4 months over 2024–2025 (METR, 2025). Capability is therefore expanding faster than the institutions meant to track its labor effects. Second, deployment is already broad rather than speculative: more than three-quarters of large firms report using AI in at least one business function (Ellingrud et al., 2023), and the World Economic Forum projects structural labor-market churn equivalent to 22 percent of today’s jobs by 2030 (World Economic Forum, 2025).

Robotics studies show that industrial robots depress wages and employment in affected local labor markets (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020). Artificial intelligence is the first technology capable of automating meaningful portions of cognitive work, particularly the entry-level and developmental work through which expertise, judgment, and professional competence have traditionally been formed. As a result, AI represents more than another wave of productivity-enhancing technology. Through automation, augmentation, and autonomous agents, it has the potential to reshape the mechanisms by which organizations develop talent, transfer knowledge, and cultivate future experts. 

Prior disruptions displaced workers from tasks while preserving the experiential pathways through which new forms of expertise emerged. New jobs were created. Labor markets adjusted. The developmental ladder held. AI disrupts that sequence at its foundation. By automating the entry-level and early-career work that has historically served as the training ground for professional judgment, AI is not merely eliminate roles, it’s dismantling the pipeline through which the next generation of experts, supervisors, and decision-makers are produced, which are needed to oversee and govern the AI and business ecosystems of the future. It documents the scale and cost of AI-driven disruption, including the pathway through which cognitive capability erodes when the work that builds it disappears. The emergence of Large Language Model (LLM) based autonomous agents represents not merely a technological advancement but a fundamental restructuring of the computational and economic landscape. This paper presents a critical examination of the emerging "Agent Economy"-the complex ecosystem of autonomous systems, human-AI collaboration, and novel economic relationships that are reshaping industries, labor markets, and organizational structures.
We examine the economic forces driving agent adoption, the nature and extent of labor market disruption, the emergence of agent marketplaces and economic primitives, and the governance challenges posed by autonomous systems. Our analysis reveals that while LLM agents offer substantial productivity gains-reportedly 30-50% efficiency improvements in knowledge work sectors-they simultaneously raise profound questions about employment, skill requirements, wealth distribution, and the future of human agency in an increasingly automated world.
We propose a novel framework for understanding human-AI labor complementarity and discuss policy interventions that could maximize benefits while mitigating potential harms. This work contributes to the growing discourse on AI economics and offers actionable insights for policymakers, business leaders, and researchers navigating this transformative period.
